Introduction

We have reached a critical moment where we now face challenges that are difficult to resolve, despite achieving technological advancements more than ever. Humanity has increased its dependence on technology by launching some 26,000 satellites into space and laying vast networks of fiber-optic cables underground on a global scale.
This age of the machine makes everything seem automated. The machines can process, predict, and generate. However, we need to understand it cannot close the loop on its own. That final step, the act of seeing with intention, and of asking critically what the machine is doing behind, still requires a human to step into the feedback loop.
This is the paradox that defines our moment. The more capable our machines become, the more urgently we are forced to ask what is distinctly human. Automation does not dissolve the question of humanity, it sharpens it. When a model can write, paint, and compose, we find ourselves asking what it means to write with a body, to paint from grief, to compose inside a dying ecosystem.
A computational art practice sits within this shifting climate of evolving technology and varying levels of opacity. Research and writing becomes part of a creative practice that investigates the tension and dimensions of existing within a technoenvironment, as well as working with computation, information, and data as artistic material and process.
The works gathered in this journal emerge from the authors’ own individual practices as MFA and MA students of Computational Arts at Goldsmiths, University of London. They explore what is quietly hollowed out beneath this current moment, the remainders that refuse to be tagged, tracked, averaged, or predicted.
They share no common brief, yet the same preoccupation surfaces again and again: a suspicion of what computation claims it can capture, and an attention to what escapes. Together they move across three territories: Bodies & Embodiment, AI & Machine Vision, Ecology & Society. The first volume f0rm1ess, we do not rely on predefined forms to express our ideas. Instead, we explore the potential that exists between digits 0 and 1. We want to push beyond the binary idea that machines are either good or bad, and explore what it looks like to collaborate with them in an almost symbiotic relationship. We do not try to locate a finite point, which can be defined as “0.5” but rather constantly shift, derive, or exist as multiples at the same time. Instead, we ask: can all ecologies ranging from DNA to computer code rather exist as abstract poles of the machinic and the organic;; as spaces where the “other than”… the “else than”… the “post-”… the “more than” circulate?

Bodies & Embodiment

In this section you will find some pieces regarding embodiment through creative technology.

Baudrillard referred to Trompe l’Oeil* as a tactile promise that doesn’t follow through, drawing a comparison between this experience and that of death.

So you are looking at a painting of a piece of paper and seeing its crease - yet being unable to reach out and crinkle it yourself. How might technology come into play with this form of dissonance?

So you are watching your hand through a VR set but it isn’t your hand at all. Is there freedom in it?

Following through on the promise of change, this section offers an examination of extending oneself and their somatic experience through multidisciplinary, multimedia experimentation and posthmanist shenanigans.

FRAN HAYES & ZIHE ZHENG

EVELUTION

A conversation between feminist cyborgs across time and space

According to technologist Blaise Agüera y Arcas, life is computational from its very inception; it emerges from systems that can self-replicate and transmit the information required to sustain existence. Under this lens, we are made of computers. We are computers. We are computers made of computers.
However, while positioning collective life as a form of intelligence, by also inciting game theory - in particular The Prisoner’s Dilemma[^1], which argues that even within a networking framework two individuals might choose not to cooperate even if it is in their best interest - Agüera y Arcas frames the collective as an optimisation strategy where individual, self-interested parts work together simply for efficiency. He clings to atomistic origins, suggesting individuals are interchangeable parts within a network.

We want to question and propose alternatives to this strict, rigid, masculine view of life and computation, views that, as stated in the publication DATA LOAM, are causing “the rise of autonomous systems whose algorithms of machine learning / artificial intelligence are deeply entangled with dubious and disintegrating forces—forces that by no means wish to make possible the prosperity and happiness of all.”[^2]
Following evolutionary biologist Lynn Margulis, we see the coming-together of life not as a corporate division of labor, but as a deeply messy, intimate entanglement of all kinds of living and non-living kin where boundaries dissolve entirely, “Life did not take over the globe by combat, but by networking”[^3]. We are not isolated processing units; we are all assemblages.
In response we welcomed symbiogenesis, the coming-together of distinct parts to form a more complex whole[^4]. Through opening our research into a space of radical feminist assemblage we conceived a speculative, symbiogenetic entity; an assemblage composed of the human mitochondrial genome - colloquially known as Mitochondrial Eve,[^5] this genome is passed exclusively through the matriarchal lineage suggesting that the entire human race can be traced back to a singular woman - the traditionally feminine craft of crochet, JavaScript code, and slime mold. Within this assemblage relationships come first, the actors do not exist as individual parts, but actively become-together through acts of entanglement that transform them.

We are asking, can viewing the symbiogenesis of different bodies[^6] and ecologies through a radically feminine, craft-based lens offer a slower, kinder alternative to the relentless, extractive pace of the current technological landscape?

The text that follows is a conversation conducted across time, space, and kin. It brings together three distinct perspectives: [MITO]: The symbiogenic organism herself; [FRAN & ZIHE]: The human developers and companion-creators of the organism; [FUTURE SWARM]: A speculative, future, hive-mind evolution of the crochet cyborg, perhaps a symbiont of its own making.
Through this polyphonic dialogue, we intend to interrogate the motives and methods behind the creation of the cyborg, to de-center its human developers, and to ask whether decentering more previously dominant (masculine) parties within our technological frameworks can shift us toward a future of deeper computational empathy and ecological respect.

[fran & zihe]
Through reading Agüera y Arcas’ book What is Intelligence? we discovered cellular automata (CA), a simulation for life-like behaviour popularised by John Conway’s Game of Life. CA functions most commonly as a two-dimensional grid of cells where each cell is affected by the state of its eight neighbouring cells.
Using JavaScript, we translated the 16,569 character human mitochondrial genome into a grid of cells, where the letters that make up the genome - ‘A’, ‘C’, ‘T’, and ‘G’ - are assigned each to one of four colours.
Using the CA algorithm, we activated this grid, creating an infinite movement of the cells. This process was mirrored with a Physarum Polycephalum (slime mold) algorithm expanded from research by Jeff Jones and Sage Jenson.

Both the algorithmically activated grids were used within a TouchDesigner (TD) patch to drive noise that simulated cell growth. This visual growth was outputted as a low resolution (30 x 30 pixel) grid of the original four colours and a white, transparent layer.
We developed our own code to translate the png files into the embodied crocheted forms, where each colour represents a different crochet stitch. Through extracting samples from the image sequence, we were able to map different stages of your evolution into a crochet form that embodies elements of human, machine and nonhuman organism.

In-Between States

Assemblage, Repetition, and the Labour of Technical Objects in Artistic Practice

Instructions:

| Choose a technical object. It should have more than one part and at least one connection that can be undone by hand. If the object has no removable parts, choose a different object. | | *The object already exists before you arrive.* | | Place the object on a clean surface. Walk around it. If you can see it from four sides, stop at each side for thirty seconds. If the object is against a wall, move it so you can reach every angle. | | *Care requires access.* | | Touch every surface you can reach. Start from the outside and move inward. If two parts meet, press the joint lightly. If the joint moves, note which direction. | | *The hands learn what the eyes skip over.* | | Find every connection. Count them. If you are unsure whether something is a connection, try to move it. If it moves, it is a connection. | | *The number of connections is the number of ways the object could fail and has not yet.* | | Choose one connection and undo it. If it requires a tool, use the smallest tool that works. Hold the two separated parts. | | *They carry the memory of having been joined and the potential of being joined again.* | | Redo the connection. If the resistance feels the same as when you undid it, the material has not yet registered your action. If the resistance feels different, it has. | | *This is the smallest unit of maintenance* | | Choose a different connection. Repeat steps 5 and 6\. If you run out of connections, return to the first one and undo it again. | | *Each repetition modifies the conditions of the next.* | | Find a surface on the object that you have never cleaned. Clean it. If there is dust, remove it. If there is residue, leave it. | | *Dust collects where care has not reached.* | | Look at every visible edge. If an edge is misaligned, adjust it. If it resists adjustment, leave it. Come back to it tomorrow. | | *If something resists, it is telling you the limits of your control.* | | Write down which connections you opened and what felt different when you closed them. If nothing felt different, write that down too. | | *The object stores its memory in its parts.* | | Return the object to the surface. Do not touch it for twenty four hours. If you feel the urge to adjust something, wait. | | *The object continues to change without you.* | | Repeat the process with another object. | | *If the repetition produces difference, the practice is alive.* |
Technical objects are often considered finished artifacts that serve a pre-determined purpose. Within an engineering logic, a system is expected to operate according to governed protocols in order to minimize errors. Control is essential. The system is designed to converge, to close the gap between its current state and its goal. Error is minimized. Noise is filtered. The technical object, under this logic, exists in service of a predetermined endpoint, and its success is measured by how efficiently it arrives there. Wiener called this cybernetics: the scientific study of control and communication in the animal and the machine.¹

If the endpoint is accepted as the goal of the work, then the entire process becomes instrumental. Every action is justified only by whether it gets you closer to the finished thing. The parts, the motors, the screws, the wires all become means, and the moment the object is complete, the process is discarded. This kills all the fun.

When I operate with a technical object, the boundary of clear authority over the system becomes intricate. I enter a space where control is shared, distributed, and often deliberately undermined. Engineering logic maximises control to converge toward a goal. Chance based art abandons control to generate complexity through randomness. Both produce a separation between the practitioner and the work: one makes the artist an executor of a plan, the other makes them a spectator to their own practice. I am interested in neither. I want to stay with the work in its various stages, sharing control with the system and sustaining that shared condition through repetition. The in between state proposed here occupies a third territory, a sustained condition where identity emerges through continuous differentiation rather than arrival at a predetermined form.

The exploded view performs something that I think Heidegger was getting at when he argued that equipment in use tends to withdraw from attention, and that only when it breaks down does its structure become visible.² To lay out the parts of a guitar across a surface is to make visible the relations that hold the object together. The joints. The screws. The connections that ordinarily withdraw into the unified form. Each part, once separated, reveals itself as a site of labour. Every screw has been tightened by someone. Every joint has been aligned by hand. The object is held together not by design alone but by accumulated acts of care.

The technical object does not exist only when assembled and functional. What Simondon calls phase is useful here: "it is the actual system of all phases taken together that is the complete reality, not each phase in itself."³ The object exists equally when its parts are distributed, when its connections are loosened, when its form is undone. The distributed parts carry the memory of having been one, and the potential of becoming one again, differently. The assembled guitar is a momentary stabilization, already anticipating its own disassembly. I have come to think of this as the object's real condition, always somewhere between together and apart, always in the middle of being maintained.

The question that keeps returning to me is one that extends what Ingold asks in his critique of the hylomorphic model of creation.⁴ He asks: what does it mean to create things? I want to push this further: what does it mean to maintain things? Because the shift from creation to maintenance changes everything. It means the work is never finished. It means the encounter with material is ongoing. It means the labour of repetition, adjustment, and care is the practice itself rather than a stage on the way to a completed object.

Ukeles understood this when she wrote her Manifesto for Maintenance Art in 1969.⁵ She drew a line between development and maintenance. Development labour produces a finished object and terminates. Maintenance labour is cyclical, endless, structurally incapable of completion. "Maintenance is a drag; it takes all the fucking time." I keep coming back to this sentence because it says something precise about the ontological condition of maintenance: it occupies all available time because it has no endpoint at which it could stop. To maintain a technical object is to enter a relationship with it that cannot be concluded. Every adjustment invites the next adjustment. Every tightened screw will loosen again.

The parts are not passive in this. They carry forward what has happened to them. Their accumulated wear, their loosened connections, their particular resistances shape what the next assembly can become. What Bolt calls material thinking, the idea that the practitioner does not think first and then make but thinks through the making itself, converges here with what Stiegler calls prosthetic memory, the way technical objects store experience outside the body.⁶ ⁷ The guitar parts are not inert matter waiting for my plan. They think back. They remember what my hands have done to them, and they push back in ways that change what I can do next. I am not the sole author of the configuration. The parts co-author it through their memory.

The artist, then, is a maintainer. Someone who stays with the system, shares control with it, and sustains the conditions under which difference can continue to emerge. Not an author who imposes form. Not a spectator who sets up conditions and steps back. A maintainer.

I should be honest about the limits of this position. If "refusing to finish" becomes a fixed formula, then the refusal of closure becomes its own form of closure. The methodology calcifies into style. The repetition stops producing difference and starts producing habit. I do not have a theoretical solution to this. The only safeguard is practical: genuine attention to whether the repetition is still producing difference or has become mechanical. Care cannot be guaranteed by a model. It can only be committed to and noticed when it fails.

What sustains all of this is care. To maintain is to repeat. To repeat is to differentiate. To differentiate is to remain in between. And to remain in between, deliberately, with attention and persistence, is to care.

End Notes

¹ Norbert Wiener, Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1948), 11.

² Martin Heidegger, Being and Time, trans. John Macquarrie and Edward Robinson (Oxford: Blackwell, 1962), 102–103.

³ Gilbert Simondon, "The Genesis of Technicity," trans. Cecile Malaspina and John Rogove, e-flux Journal, no. 82 (May 2017).

⁴ Tim Ingold, Making: Anthropology, Archaeology, Art and Architecture (London: Routledge, 2013), 21.

Huayang Lei

Beyond the Organic

Emergent Umwelt and Indeterminacy in Embodied Computational Systems

Living organisms are typically understood as autonomous entities that sense, respond to, and adapt to their surroundings, while artificial systems are regarded as passive tools executing predetermined instructions. Developments in cybernetics, artificial life, and computational art increasingly unsettle this division. This essay asks whether a non-biological system can develop an operational Umwelt through embodied interaction with its environment, and answers on conceptual grounds. An Umwelt is not a pre-given setting but a relational structure emerging through the interplay of perception, action, memory, and feedback. And this emergence is not purely computational, since embodiment is the condition under which a system meets a world, it has not itself specified. Drawing on von Uexküll, theories of emergence, and feminist science studies, the argument is developed conceptually and then instantiated in a computational installation of my own. On this basis, the boundary between the biological and the artificial requires reconsideration.

1. Umwelt: The World as Selectively Constructed

Jakob von Uexküll proposed that every organism inhabits its own Umwelt, a world constituted through its capacities for perception and action (von Uexküll 2010). His tick, drawn to warmth and the scent of butyric acid, does not perceive a reduced version of the human world but a different world altogether, built only from the signals that matter to it. An environment, then, is not simply given. What counts as a creature’s world is not the totality of information around it but the narrow set of features its body renders meaningfully. The Umwelt is constructed rather than received. Uexküll developed this for biological organisms, yet its logic does not obviously stop there. If an Umwelt arises through selective perception and interaction rather than through life as such, must such a world remain biological, or can a non-biological system, sensing through its own narrow channels, construct an operational Umwelt of its own?

2. Emergence, Cybernetics, and the Production of Agency

In complexity science, emergence describes higher-order behaviour arising from interactions among simple components rather than from central instruction: Conway’s Game of Life and von Neumann’s cellular automata generate organised patterns that no single rule specifies (von Neumann 1966). Organisation can be produced through relation rather than imposed. Cybernetics locates the same principle in the coupling between system and surroundings. For Wiener (1948), behaviour is not a linear chain of cause and effect but a circuit of feedback, sensing, responding, and continually modifying one’s relation to an environment. Agency is enacted through recursive exchange rather than housed in a substance. This principle has a lineage in cybernetic art: Gordon Pask’s The Colloquy of Mobiles (1968) comprised suspended units that communicated through light and sound and adapted to one another, so that collective behaviour arose from interaction rather than from any script. Read together, these accounts suggest an Umwelt need not precede a system. It can instead be understood as an emergent property of the system’s own activity: a relational structure produced through perception, action, and feedback, the environment emerging with the system rather than waiting for it.

3. Can an Environment Be Purely Computational?

This shift from representing life to staging the conditions under which life-like behavior emerges has been pursued in robotic installations such as Rinaldo’s Autopoiesis (2000). But it invites a sharper objection. Agüera y Arcas (2025a, 2025b) argues that life and intelligence are fundamentally computational and demonstrates the claim through experiments in which random code spontaneously evolves into self-replicating programs. Life-like dynamics emerging from computation alone, with no body and no physical environment. If life can arise purely in code, why insist on embodiment? Why would a digital agent running the same perception–action loop not possess an Umwelt of its own?

The answer lies in distinguishing a limited set of channels from a closed world. A computational agent’s environment is a state space its designer has already specified; nothing in it exceeds what was encoded. A physical system’s channels may be equally narrow, but the world they reach into is not, which is co-produced by a room, by passing bodies, by changes the system cannot fully predict. Limited channels are not a closed world.

Here feminist science studies become decisive. Arcas treats life as competitive dynamics in an abstract informational space, a framing Hayles (1999) identifies as the historical erasure of embodiment, the assumption that information can exist independently of any material substrate. Barad’s (2007) notion of intra-action sharpens the alternative: agency is not possessed prior to relation but emerges within material entanglement. Embodiment is therefore not a redundant constraint but the condition under which a system meets a world it has not itself specified.

4. Case Study: An Installation as Instantiation

To ground the argument, I built an installation as a minimal embodied system that senses and acts through two narrow channels: the colour of ambient light and the proximity of nearby bodies. Its world is deliberately impoverished. Following Uexküll, what matters is not how much it registers but which features become meaningful for it, and this selectivity is something the system enacts, not something given to it.

The channels are limited, but the world they reach is not. The colour sensor reads light shaped by the room, by passing visitors, and by the light the system itself emits; the rangefinder responds to movements it cannot anticipate. The system acts by emitting light that its own sensor then reads, coupling source and sensor within a shared space (Figure 1), so that changing the colour it produces changes the colour it next perceives. This closes the recursive loop, perception, action, environmental change, new perception, which is a physical circuit rather than a metaphor.

A slowly drifting baseline adds memory: salience is computed relative to an accumulated history rather than an absolute value, so identical input can prompt different responses over time. The installation thus instantiates the paper’s claims directly, an Umwelt selectively constructed, relationally produced, and dependent on embodiment for its coupling to an unspecified world.

Figure 2. [description of the installation]

5. Rethinking of the Biological Boundary

If an Umwelt emerges through relation rather than biological substance, the line between living and artificial systems grows unstable. What seems unique to organisms may depend less on organic material than on the capacity to enter dynamic relations with a world. This does not make the installation alive. It suggests that agency and environmental engagement lie along a continuum rather than within a binary , and that embodied computational systems matter because they expose this ambiguity rather than resolve it.

6. Conclusion

An Umwelt, this paper has argued, is not a pre-given environment but a relational structure produced through embodied interaction. Drawing on Uexküll, cybernetics, and feminist science studies, and instantiated in an installation of my own, it has held that meaningful environmental relations can emerge in a non-biological system. Not because life reduces to computation, but because such relations require a body coupling to a world it has not specified. Such systems do not merely occupy environments. They help produce them. The boundary between the biological and the artificial therefore calls for reconsideration.

Yiho

What Passes Through

A Genealogy of Portals from Sight to Body

From Boundary to Seamlessness: Does Fascination with Elsewhere Disappear?

Having worked in XR for years, I have always been fascinated by the possibility of stepping into other worlds. Looking back, I realised this fascination began long before I ever put on a headset. As a child, I was captivated by stories built around impossible passages between worlds. I dreamed of running through the brick wall of Platform 9¾ like Harry Potter, stepping through Doraemon's Anywhere Door, falling down the rabbit hole with Alice, and crawling through the coats of an old wardrobe into Narnia.

By 2026, the development of technology heavily emphasizes a "frictionless" society, which is an era where spatial computing and mixed reality strive to seamlessly integrate the virtual into our physical environment. However, without a sense of boundary, does this seamless actualization kill the magic of our imagination? When virtual entities merge perfectly into our living rooms, becoming those simulated landscapes, lovers, furniture or pets, does the imaginary world risk losing its aura as an "elsewhere", dissolving into just another extension of the “here”?

Therefore, discussing the concept of the “portal” is more urgent than ever. In this text, I trace the genealogy of the portal across two primary dimensions, separated by a crucial turning point: the advent of the video game and the realization of player agency.

The first dimension, “the medium itself as portal”, focuses on the pre-interactive era, exploring how the presence of a “framed” boundary in traditional arts sustains our longing for an “elsewhere”. The second dimension, which also builds upon the first dimension, “the digital portal in virtual worlds” enables us to focus on how the term “portal” itself has now emerged directly within video games and VR/MR as an interactive object, and how the player can “enter” to the “elsewhere”.

Furthermore, through my own artistic practice independently and as an art collective, CURIOSKI, I will talk about how crossing a portal has transformed into a deeply embodied process in the headset where the physical body itself is required to immerse into new realities.

The Pre-Interactive Era: When Portals Belonged to Sight

First, look at how boundaries in the arts frame our longing for an “elsewhere”. Before the advent of interactive digital media, the portal was still only a window within the medium itself. In architecture, illusionistic ceiling painting, the so-called “Trompe-l'œil”, or Quadratura, in the cathedral serves as a classic example. By dissolving the physical ceiling into an infinite sky, it invites the eye to ascend into a spiritual world.

As for paintings, John Berger in Ways of Seeing notes, "perspective makes the single eye the centre of the visible world" (Berger 1972, 16). That is, everything in the painting is set out for our sight, and the viewer is always kept outside the picture frame as a physical boundary. Paintings like Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait or Petrus Christus's A Goldsmith in His Shop seem to push against this, using a convex mirror as a small meta-portal that reflects the space in front of the picture and appears to pull our world inside. However, such visual tricks still cannot eliminate the fact that the reality is blocked outside the picture frame.

René Magritte pushes this play with the boundary even further. In La Condition Humaine, an easel stands in front of a window, and the painted canvas upon it continues the landscape outside so seamlessly that we cannot tell where the real view ends and the picture begins. Yet in his series of doors, such as La Réponse Imprévue, L'acte de Foi, a closed door is broken but open by an irregular hole that reveals the space behind it. The frame as a portal is no longer something we merely look into, but a threshold we desire to step through, which the screen, and later the headset, will take up in earnest to realise.

Watching Others Cross: The Diegetic Portal on Movie Screen

With the arrival of the screen, portals begin to proliferate as diegetic objects within the story. In this context, we are no longer pointing solely at the framed medium itself, but at the impossible passages that open up inside the story such as a magic wardrobe, a rift in space, or even a stargate. The theorist of modern media culture, Anne Friedberg argues in her book, The Virtual Window, “the cinematic screen is a paradoxical window: it gives the viewer a mobilized, virtual gaze that seems to travel between worlds, even as the body stays seated in the dark (Friedberg 2006)”. Indeed, while characters traverse “passages” in the film, for the audience, the editing cut itself functions as another invisible portal for their eyes, letting them rely on psychological empathy to put themselves in a story unfolding in some distant “elsewhere”.

However, it is the video game that takes the next radical step: what crosses the portal is no longer merely our sight, but an avatar under our direct control.

Beyond the Screen in Games: Interactive Portals and Avatar Agency

Speaking of games, the portal becomes the classic interactive metaphor for player agency. In fact, the concept of the "portal" is deeply rooted in video game terminology as a fundamental mechanic for avatar’s navigation. In the earlier games like Super Mario Bros, portals like “Warp Pipes” only served as symbolic gateways used to transition between game levels. While they offered access to hidden routes or shortcuts, their function remained passive and fixed within the game's spatial structure.

By contrast, in a more contemporary game like Portal 2, portals are transformed into an active tool for manipulating spaces. Players can strategically place portals to circumvent physical constraints and redirect momentum, for example, converting vertical free-fall energy into horizontal velocity when they are navigating in a 3D space.

To understand how portals redefine spatial structure in rendering, we must look into “Non-Euclidean geometry”. While traditional Euclidean space relies on absolute constants of distance and proportion, game designers can utilize the portal as a “spatial editor”. For instance, players may encounter chambers that are internally larger than their external dimensions, and having a “'TARDIS-like” feeling, or experience self-folding infinite loops in one space. This manipulation of topology turns what would be a static, enclosed room into a generative, malleable structure.

Portals are no longer destinations to be traversed; they become tools through which players actively reshape their spatial environment. At the same time, it anticipates contemporary VR/MR experiences where space itself becomes a mutable and interactive medium.

Dissolving the Frame in VR: The Headset as the Portal Itself

Before VR headsets came out, what passed through the portal into the "elsewhere" was only the viewer's sight, or at most their game avatar. The viewer always remained an outsider, peering in some kind of frame, either a picture's frame, or a screen. The VR headset, however, seals off reality altogether: once the display wraps a full 360 degrees around the eyes, what crosses into the "elsewhere" is, for the first time, the body itself.

What changes most on this virtual side of the portal is how we feel about our own body because we never reach the edge of the virtual space. As Jaron Lanier observes through his notion of homuncular flexibility, the brain's internal map of the body, its body schema is not fixed, so once a body is remapped in VR, we can learn to inhabit and control a form quite unlike our own (Lanier 2017).

In my past work Low-life, I turned the viewer into a non-human body—a cockroach in a kitchen—where the world is seen from a low, ground-level vision, through a perspective our own bodies could never inhabit. Similarly, in CURIOSKI, one of my collective’s projects, A Glimpse of the Mind Landscape, we treated the headset itself as a “mind-plugin”. We explored how consciousness interacts with different states of embodiment, including human forms, mysterious creatures, and even existence without any body at all.

Bringing the “Elsewhere” Closer in MR: Virtual Portals in Physical Reality

Moving to the mixed reality(MR), it becomes harder to say that the headset itself is the portal, because MR no longer clearly separates an inside from an outside (the virtual world vs. the reality). Here the discussion of the portal can be focused from the whole headset down to a threshold opened within the scene. Making an MR experience in a game engine like Unity, for example, we can design how exactly transparent the real world should be seen, and how our real body can trigger a simulated door, for the player to move back and forth between the reality and the virtual world.

The realization of these bidirectional portals relies fundamentally on the "pass-through" technology of contemporary headsets, such as the Meta Quest 3 or Apple Vision Pro. When we put on the headset, our physical vision is completely enclosed at first, then, the "reality" will be rendered in a real-time, digitized reconstruction captured by external cameras and projected onto screens inside the headset.

CURIOSKI's The Insider takes this up as a narrative practice, assembling physical and virtual objects into a single space: we placed a virtual window on the real wall through which one could look out. On the other hand, in Paxville, we did the opposite—making holes around the reality to look into the virtual world behind it. The two works map the two directions a portal can open in MR, emphasizing this threshold connecting “here” and “there”, is no longer merely transporting us, but collapsing the boundary between the two, allowing physical reality and virtual imagination to seamlessly blend into one another.

The Unfinished Imagination of the Elsewhere

Tracing the genealogy of the portal reveals that humanity has always had that fantasy to imaginary worlds before and after the technological era. The portal is simply the evolving vessel for this profound longing. From the painted sky of a cathedral ceiling, to painter's canvases, to the moving image of film, to the digital gateways an avatar can cross in games, to the VR headset the body itself can enter, and finally to mixed reality, which pulls the virtual into our physical world—the medium changes, and so does what passes through, from sight, to avatar, to body.

The portal's magic was not arrival, but the way to reach it. What we are sure of is that our exploration into the “elsewhere” will continue forever.

End Notes

Fioretta Zhang

Onycho Lab Artificial Nails as Bodily Technology

How do we define the boundary of the human body?

This question began for me with a daily life experience: wearing long artificial nails. Every time I get nail extensions, my hands feel strange for at least two or three weeks. My fingers seem longer than before. The distance I can reach changes. My gestures become slower, more cautious, sometimes less functional. I type differently, pick up objects differently, and touch surfaces with a slightly altered awareness. When the nails are removed, my body must recalibrate again. My fingers feel shorter. The world seems to return to a previous distance. This small cosmetic modification produces a temporary illusion: my brain begins to treat an artificial extension as part of the body.

Artificial Nails as Interactable Wearable Device

What it means to body has been redefined by technologies that are increasingly absorbed into everyday embodiment. I was inspired by Andy Clark’s concept of mind extension.[^1] We understand that tools and technologies act as continuous extensions of the human mind and body. However, artificial nails complicate this functionalist narrative. Clark argues that an external entity coupled to our body qualifies as an extension of our mind if it performs a function that is sufficiently similar to an internal cognitive process. When we rely on a notebook to store information that we would otherwise remember, the notebook becomes an extension of the mind because it occupies the same functional role as biological memory.

I accept the spirit of Clark's thesis, but I argue that functional equivalence is not the only basis for extension. An external object may become part of the body or mind not by replicating an existing function but by reorganizing the body's functional capacities in ways that the body comes to treat as its own. Artificial nails illustrate this alternative. Unlike the notebook, they do not simply enhance or imitate the functions of biological nails or fingers. Yet their significance lies precisely in their capacity to reorganize bodily action. As the wearer adapts, the brain recalibrates motor planning so that movements are executed as if the artificial nails were part of the hand itself. The body thus reorganizes its functional architecture around the external object. What legitimizes the artificial nails as an extension of the body is therefore not functional equivalence but functional integration through reorganization.

To explore this idea, I created Onycho Lab: a performative computational installation that asks how an seemingly insignificant, decorative object can reconfigure the human body’s perception of its own boundaries.

After multiple prototyping, I developed a wearable haptic feedback system to symbolically modify this extension. The computational mechanism is intentionally localized. Micro-pressure sensors are embedded at the distal tip of the artificial nail, acting as synthetic nerve endings. When the extension makes physical contact with a surface, the sensor triggers a tiny vibration motor adhered to the dorsal side, the back, of the biological finger. By displacing the site of impact from the tip of the prosthetic to the skin of the wearer, the system creates a closed sensation loop. The artificial nail, therefore, becomes an interactable wearable device.

Between Salon and Clinic

Beyond the wearable device, the work also recognizes manicure as a body-modification procedure. Manicure is normally understood as a beauty service, an act of care, or a commercial ritual associated with femininity and self-presentation. Yet if we look closely, the process of manicure shares a similar procedural structure with medical intervention. Before entering the space, one often makes an appointment, clarifies needs and expectations, discloses relevant bodily information, and prepares for a treatment. During the procedure, the hand is disinfected, examined, held still, and worked upon with specialised tools. Something may be removed from the body, such as cuticle, skin, or nail surface; something may be added, such as gel, extension, colour, or structure. The body is modified through expertise.

Of course, manicure and surgery are not identical. Their risks, legal status, institutional authority, and social meanings are radically different. Onycho Lab stages manicure as a performative surgery in order to reveal the procedural and political structures that are already present within beauty work. Both manicure and surgery involve intimate bodily access. Both require trust. Both depend on tools, hygiene, technical knowledge, and the temporary passivity of the person being touched. Both can be caring, but both can also be controlling. Both transform the body through a relation of expertise. The difference lies in the degree.

Given the above functional resemblance, the authority, power, and status of the doctor and the manicurist is still valued very differently. Medical touch is protected by institutional power, professional status, and the language of necessity. Manicure touch is often feminised, commercialised, racialised, and dismissed as service labour. Yet the body does not experience this labour as trivial. The hand must still be surrendered. The client must still remain still. The practitioner still shapes, cuts, files, attaches, and corrects. The apparent softness of beauty service can conceal a complex choreography of bodily compliance.

This observation motivated me to design an installation setting that sits between a salon, a clinic, and a laboratory. The project was created as a performative computational installation that reprograms the ordinary act of manicure into a body-modification procedure. Participants enter a staged environment that sits between a nail salon, a clinic, and a laboratory. They are invited to book or enter an appointment, read basic information, sign a consent form, and offer their hand for a procedure. I perform as a fictional haptic doctor: masked, gloved, emotionally restrained, and precise in gesture. The participant sits under intense light while their hand is held, positioned, fitted, and tested. What begins as a familiar beauty service gradually becomes displaced into something more clinical, more procedural, and more ambiguous.

Onycho Lab brings the conflict among clinics and salons into the installation environment. Translucent white gauze surrounds the space, creating a semi-private and semi-public enclosure. From the outside, viewers can only vaguely glimpse the procedure inside, as if witnessing something intimate but not fully accessible. From within, participants temporarily detach from the ordinary exhibition space and enter a fictional clinical field. Strong spotlights illuminate the participant’s hand. Disinfectant scent intensifies the medical atmosphere. My masked face and doctor’s uniform produce an invisible pressure.

Consent, Care, and Feminist Hapticism

I also designed a consent form for my performative installation. The consent form marks the point at which the participant formally allows their body to be altered. Body modification needs consent because it involves touch, bodily access, technical intervention, and care. The participant is not only looking at an artwork. Their hand is held, positioned, touched, fitted, and modified. Their body becomes the site of the work.

Through this project, I discovered that manicure and surgery both include a form of care, but care is not always good for the person being cared for. Care can be intimate, supportive, and protective, but it can also be disciplinary, corrective, and controlling. Both manicure and surgery involve the temporary surrender of the body to another person’s expertise. Both can be performed in the name of improvement. Both can transform the body through touch. Therefore, care should not be treated as automatically ethical. Care should require consent.

This is where Foucault’s concept of biopolitics becomes useful. Foucault argues that political power does not only operate by forbidding or punishing bodies, but by regulating, organising, optimising, and managing life. In a similar vein, manicure can also be understood as a small-scale form of bodily regulation. It shapes how the hand should appear, how the body should be maintained, and how femininity, cleanliness, beauty, and self-care are performed. Manicure seems soft and decorative, but it also participates in the regulation of bodily norms. It files, corrects, extends, polishes, and disciplines the body through care.

Therefore, manicure should require consent not only because it touches the body, but because it participates in the social and technical regulation of the body. The question is not whether manicure is as serious as surgery. The question is why some forms of bodily modification are recognised as requiring consent, while other feminised and cosmetic forms of modification are treated as ordinary service.

Yet the work also questions whether consent can ever be reduced to a single signature. The participant may agree before the procedure begins, but their feelings may shift as the nail is attached, as the motor vibrates, as their hand is held, or as they become aware of being observed. Consent becomes an ongoing bodily negotiation rather than a fixed administrative moment.

This is why feminist hapticism becomes necessary. I understand feminist hapticism not simply as a celebration of touch against patriarchal visual hegemony or ocularcentrism, but as a skeptical framework for analysing how touch is organised. Touch is never neutral. It is shaped by gendered labour, social roles, institutional protocols, material arrangements, and the unequal distribution of authority. Touch can care, but it can also discipline. It can create intimacy, but it can also expose vulnerability. It can heal, beautify, measure, correct, or control.

The reversibility of touch is central to this framework. To touch is always also to be touched. This reversibility challenges the stable boundary between subject and object, active and passive, practitioner and recipient. In Onycho Lab, the participant touches the world through the artificial nail, but is also touched by the device, by the performer, by the clinical atmosphere, and by the institutional fiction of the procedure. The work does not treat tactility as automatically ethical or liberating. Instead, it asks who has the right to touch the body, who authorises its transformation, and under what conditions modification becomes acceptable.

When the procedure ends and the sensors are detached, the body remembers everything.

End Notes

  • Clark, Andy, Natural-Born Cyborgs: Minds, Technologies, and the Future of Human Intelligence (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2003)

  • Foucault, Michel, The Birth of Biopolitics: Lectures at the Collège de France, 1978–1979, trans. by Graham Burchell (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2008)

  • Kang, Miliann, The Managed Hand: Race, Gender, and the Body in Beauty Service Work (Berkeley: University of California Press, 2010)

  • Merleau-Ponty, Maurice, Phenomenology of Perception, trans. by Colin Smith (London: Routledge & Kegan Paul, 1962)---- more specific Chiasm

  • Puig de la Bellacasa, María, Matters of Care: Speculative Ethics in More Than Human Worlds (Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press, 2017)

  • Wegenstein, Bernadette, The Cosmetic Gaze: Body Modification and the Construction of Beauty (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2012)

AI, Machine Vision & Algorithms

In the age of artificial intelligence, machine vision and algorithms, images are no longer only objects that we look at. They are also processed, classified, ranked and circulated by computational systems. This means that images do not only represent meaning; they may also influence our attention, emotions, behaviour and beliefs.

This section discusses how AI and machine vision change the ways images are seen, produced and understood. We do not treat AI as a neutral tool. Instead, we ask further questions: How do machines recognise, classify, predict and act through images? What happens when “seeing” is no longer only a human activity? What does it mean when images have already been read by machines before they are read by us?

Drawing on the questions raised by Trevor Paglen in How to See Like a Machine, we may need to ask not only what an image means, or whether it is real or fake, but also what it is doing. What kind of response is it trying to trigger? What does it make visible, and what does it simplify, misread or erase?

The following texts approach these questions from different artistic and critical perspectives. Together, they discuss the gap between human perception and machine perception, the friction between technological promises and lived experience, and the relationship between algorithmic classification and the complexity of identity, culture and subjectivity.

Jemila Abdulai

The Vampire Machine: AI in the creation of art

Why AI art does not sit well with me

I vaguely remember the first time I came across an artwork made with AI. It was a short film with impressive graphics. It had vibrant and captivating moving images that morphed from one scene to the next. I was in awe. I began to feel the shared sense of excitement in the air at the time, excited for the possibilities for making my own short films.
As someone who at the time never thought I could ever make these impressive and technically complex artworks myself, AI seemed like the perfect avenue for me to get closer to a world I had always wanted to be a part of. Now about two years later, I have moved quite far onto the opposite side of the spectrum about the use of AI models in art. In fact, I often find myself feeling a negative reaction I can't quite articulate properly yet, when I come across these same kinds of artworks browsing online or on social media today.

The term ‘AI’ (Artificial Intelligence)[^1] has been used to describe ‘the capability of computational systems to perform tasks typically associated with human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, and decision-making.’ However in recent years, due to the rise of Generative AI models such as ChatGPT and Midjourney, AI is known for a different purpose- making art.
Upon its initial introduction to the masses, Generative AI models seemed to be the future. The newest breakthrough in human technology, the ‘inevitable’ turn in human history that was supposed to fix all our problems.
Suddenly it was everywhere, and as someone who was always more of a techno-optimist, I thought this was a great turn of events. All too soon however, AI was everywhere – and not in a good way.
Almost every new tech startup launched was now an AI startup; and established companies that typically had nothing to do with technology were suddenly making ‘AI-driven strategy’ pivots; like they were trying to wedge AI assistants into any part of their business model they could.

On social media, there were many more ads pushing all the ways this shiny new technology made life so much better; with some even advertising a frankly dystopian product called ‘Friend’[^2]. This is a pendant embedded with an AI ‘companion’ you could wear around your neck and served as a partner to converse with day-to-day. Needless to say, it was not very well received by a lot of people, judging from the vandalism and graffiti it received on its ads around the city of New York.[^3] Even in my personal life, the name ‘ChatGPT’ was everywhere, with people starting to refer to the LLM using anthropomorphised terms like ‘He/She’. Even more alarmingly, it was becoming more normalised to ask it for advice about things like where to visit on holiday, what to eat for dinner or even what to do about the issues you were having with a friend. With this in mind, I started to realise how embedded it was becoming in our day to day lives; and often not by choice.

Within the world of art, the ‘AI aesthetic’ emerged and along with it came the realisation for many artists that their works were being stolen and used to train these models to produce content without their consent. In light of this, the wave of anti-AI sentiment became even more visible within the creative spaces I navigated. It was more common to label someone as ‘not a real artist’ if they had used AI in creating an artwork. Even the mention of AI in a creative context was regularly met with hostility and disdain.
The topic has become something very polarising today, with still no clear consensus about the legality of using models that have been trained with stolen or copyrighted artworks to create art. Without a doubt however, it’s safe to say the impact of AI on artists has been quite profound.

The loss of intellectual property is another outcome of the AI boom that must be discussed. Due to the aforementioned lack of legal clarity of using AI to produce art works, notions of authorship are often unclear and debatable. The referenced paper ‘The GPT Judge’ further explores this topic in further detail[^4].

Consequently, the phenomenon of cognitive offloading is another aspect of the AI boom that is increasingly becoming more and more evident.
The outcome is clear - AI is making us lazier; according to a paper published by Fayaz et al[^5]. For some artists, using AI sometimes means offloading the essential tasks of art making such as ideation and execution to these LLMs in the name of efficiency and optimisation.

One of the most important parts of being an artist is the ability to be able to develop ideas in a way that feels subversive and meaningful; by being able to question and break norms and potentially collaborate with others to do so. Art has largely been used as a vehicle for change in our society.

However it seems increasingly, some relatively renowned artists do not resonate with that, which to me was unexpected. Upon listening to a talk by the artist called ‘niceaunties’[^6] who almost predominantly uses AI tools to make their work, something seemed amiss to me. Hearing them talk about how much nicer it is to work with AI because it ‘doesn't get angry when you ask for changes’ or how ‘the line of production has shrunk and therefore become more efficient’ is something that feels out of place for a practice that seeks to challenge, explore and question things. The artist here in question describes their own practice as intended to ‘rewrite the stories of women’ making them ‘unapologetically free’. However, it seemed ironic to me to use a generative AI tool like KlingAI or Seedance to ‘rewrite stories’ when a major problem with AI is that it is regressive in nature.

AI models are often trained to operate on probability - meaning they operate by comparing what ‘is’ to what has already been. Google itself mentions using the Bayesian model[^7] as part of training its models, leading us to believe that common AI models are trained to always bring the output back to what exists and what has been done before. The outcome of this current model is that a lot of art ends up looking the same, because these models are drawing from the same probability distributions and end up simply producing the ‘average sum’ of a piece of artwork, based on all of the ones that exist in its dataset. In my opinion, this makes it quite static in nature. It easily becomes a restricting force for an artist wanting to try something new, because it is so heavily based on reading information from previously gathered datasets.
AI is not easily able to create new arguments for norms to be rewritten and deviated from. When artists use it, they often cannot break out from the norm and question things, which arguably is one of the core purposes for art creation.

A lot of modern artists increasingly rely on technology or even ‘non-human’ collaborators to produce ideas and make art which is not a problem in itself. As a computational artist myself, I believe combining art and technology is a wonderful way to allow artists to question things in ways they may have not been able to do before, and be more audacious with their work. However, the problem arises when the artist becomes increasingly detached from the ideation, execution and implementation of an artwork. There, one begins to wonder whether the outcome is truly something we can consider to be ‘art’. If they are detached from questioning the outputs of the tools - which are often designed by non-artists for artists, they risk falling into and perpetuating the ideals and imaginations of these people, which unfortunately are increasingly resonating more and more with fascist fantasies of society. Art is a process through which artists can think critically and question things, even the tools they use themselves.

Jenna Sutela’s[^8] work ‘nimiia cétiï’ is a brilliant and imaginative example of this. Her work uses machine learning, neural networks and bacteria to open up a dialogue about communication that is rich and unique.
Holly Herndon’s spawning ceremonies[^9] where people gather to willingly use their voices as training data show an interesting example of a collective and consensual collaboration between humans and an AI model.
Chipo Mapondera[^10] is another artist who uses an AI model in a subversive and thought-provoking way. She similarly operates in a collective; joining arms with members of different African indigenous cultures and a culturally rooted ‘AI climate oracle’ to help fill in the gaps of parts of their heritages that have been lost. Her works are developed closely with choreographers, archivists and ‘knowledge keepers’ whose main goal is ‘telling Indigenous stories’.

In my point of view, we must first start by asking ‘what is art and is AI art actually art?[^11]’ Who is art for? Why does it need to be optimised?’.
Additionally, we must question what purpose the creation of art serves; is it solely for generating income or for questioning the norm and imagining the world in a different way? Art is a way to express our thoughts and emotions, to communicate, and to connect with one another on the basis of our shared human experience. It doesn't seem right as an artist to create your own echo chamber of thoughts and narratives, completely disconnected from the reality of day to day life; devoid of the quality of human experience, just because it’s ‘more efficient’.

I strongly believe in the idea that there is no efficiency in creation.
In an ideal world, there should be very little place for trying to be efficient in the creative process because efficiency and producing should not be the goal. The toil of ideation and creation for an artist is a worthwhile process that should not be fast-tracked. If we ‘try to do everything efficiently, we are turning off the power of serendipity’[^12]. As Dimacali mentions in their article on AI Art ‘just because we can, doesn't mean we should’[^13]. AI is further perpetuating the capitalist mindset within art spaces that the purpose of creating art is for the market, or that production and scale are the end goal. The effect of this way of thinking on art and artists tries to rationalise it as a matter of fact.
Despite this, we need to keep reminding ourselves about the purpose that art is intended to serve, before allowing this mentality to further creep into spaces where they are actively causing damage.

Indeed, the impact of AI is a serious societal and needless to mention - environmental issue[^14]. Despite this, we must all tackle it with a shared vision to protect the rights of artists and the general developmental and intellectual well-being of our society.
All things considered, the first major steps we need to take as a society are to create regulations to protect artists and put safety measures in place that actually have the best interest of the wider community at the center. Leaving these decisions at the hands of the CEOs of big tech companies who seem to have less and less interest in being humane and socially conscious is a guaranteed way for things to spin even more out of control.

Before we accept using AI in the artistic creation process, AI models as they are need a massive overhaul. No more should they be these massive, extractive[^15] black holes of data, flattening identities and consuming any form of input to the extent of even cannibalising themselves[^16]. Perhaps it might be better to create smaller, more intentional models whose data sets have been more ethically produced and gathered. Models created for a specific purpose, either by the artists themselves or in collaboration with others in their network. This helps to challenge the assumption about whether all things can truly be categorised into text labels in the first place.
The purpose of technology should not be trying to ‘solve’ art and make it repeatable or scalable; it should be to provide artists with a way of generating questions that they didn't have before.

Although AI currently seems to be advancing at a speed that feels overwhelming to imagine attempting to control and regulate, we all deserve to live, work and create in spaces that intrinsically support, rather than detract from our creativity and expression; and therefore our human experience itself.

Yiran Jiao

Bypassing

An Empty Judgment Produced by Technology

Imagine that one day, you are told that an algorithmic risk system has placed you on a watchlist. Your past records, your place of residence, your social relations: this set of quantifiable features is close enough to those of a certain high-risk group; and so, even though you may not have committed any illegal act, you still receive a determination about yourself: a score, a risk level, contact from the police. This system, Chicago's "Strategic Subject List," ran for several years before it was shut down.¹ So what I want to ask is: why can an operational result about an individual be produced before that individual's concrete action has even taken place, and change the way they are treated?

¹ The "Strategic Subject List" is taken here as an example because it is a closed case that has already run its full course and can be looked back on; but this logic did not end when it was shut down. Similar predictive tracking, targeting, and risk-determination systems are still widely deployed today across different contexts. What this essay is concerned with is their shared structure, not the specific circumstances of any single deployment.

1. Judgment

To see clearly what this system does to judgment, we must first describe the old structure of judgment. Following Mireille Hildebrandt's account of the "informational" character of law[^1], modern legal judgment is organized around actions that have already taken place, not around some persistent state of the subject. Concrete action is the object of judgment: a person can anticipate in advance that signing a contract and then failing to perform it may bring liability, precisely because the connection between "action and consequence" lets the meaning of a behaviour be grasped before it unfolds and confirmed after it unfolds. Reasons are the mediation through which an action can be interpreted; a transfer of money may be fraud, may be support of a dependent, may be repayment of a debt, and the same external behaviour points to different structures of responsibility under different reasons. Context is the background through which action and reasons can be read. These three together support the whole structure.

At the same time, Hildebrandt adds a feature that is crucial to what follows: judgment can be modified. It is not a result that forms once and is thereby closed, but a process continually reopened by new actions, facts, and explanations. [^2]The subject's later behaviour flows back, and can loosen the initial handling. Even an everyday prejudgment based on accent or clothing is no more neutral than an algorithmic score; but it takes place within a concrete scene, and a person can resist it with action. This capacity to be reopened is precisely what keeps judgment open to the correction of itself.

2. "Judgment"

Now return to the "Strategic Subject List." Its operational logic is to infer future risk from past data. A person's records, location, risk of victimisation, and social relations are entered into the model, in order to calculate the possibility that they will become a shooting victim or perpetrator in the future. The person placed on the list may never have carried out any violent act; they may not even have done anything in the present scene that needs to be examined. They enter the system only because their data position is close enough to that of a certain high-risk group. What Antoinette Rouvroy and Thomas Berns call the "profile" comes into play here: what the system makes contact with is a statistical position recomposed from digital traces and everyday trajectories.[^3] These materials strictly belong to the past, and often do not belong to the subject's own actions: a high score may originate from the neighbourhood they lived in a few years ago, or from several records of co-appearing with a marked person. It is thin in attribution. What it records is a network position. What the subject did as an agent barely enters the calculation. And so the three conditions are absent one by one:

Concrete action disappears: the basis for handling this person is a calculated closeness to future risk, and has nothing to do with what they did.

Reasons disappear: what the model gives is correlation, a relation of co-occurrence between data points, and it cannot be refuted or corrected the way an interpretation of reasons can.

Context disappears, or rather is displaced: the background is past data compressed into features, and it often belongs to a group: the crime rate of a neighbourhood, the statistical profile of a category of population, while the consequences fall on the individual.

And at the same time, that capacity to "be reopened" is also absorbed in reverse. If a person marked as high-risk later carries out no violence, this does not overturn the handling of them. It can be read as the risk having never existed, or as the risk having already been preemptively intervened in, and either way, the score is preserved. The subject's later behaviour, their appeals, and even the fact that "the predicted behaviour never happened" are all absorbed as inputs into the model's next round of self-optimisation. What once could reopen judgment is converted into material that makes the system more precise and therefore more impossible to hold accountable. The channel of correction becomes a device that reinforces the initial handling.

This is the structure I want to call "empty judgment. "Recent work on predictive justice describes the same phenomenon. Quattrocolo (2026) discusses a case in which a traffic stop was initiated solely because it took place in an area that a predictive model had marked in advance as "high-risk." [^4]The court noted that this mode of enforcement had shifted policing away from judgment grounded in individualized suspicion, toward a preemptive logic rooted in prediction rather than concrete suspicion. Judgment is still operating, complete and efficient, with classification, contact, intervention, and consequences all falling on the subject. But the action that was its object, the reasons that were its mediation, the context that let it be read, and the openness that kept it modifiable no longer pass through the subject, no longer need the subject's building and repair; in their place, an external eye examines and measures the distance between the subject and each of the standards.

So technology opens a wormhole at the very place where judgment used to unfold. The stretch of process that should have been held up by action, that should have taken shape slowly in time and in waiting, is bypassed whole, hollowed out, and pressed flat. At the same time, whenever this wormhole meets a person's appeals against it, it rejects them completely, and goes on pulling those appeals in, turning them into material that makes it more solid, ignoring every effort that tries to change it. And what do all these bypassed things stand for, these actions, reasons, and contexts?—I take them to be precisely the conditions that depend on a span of time that has not yet arrived, that depend on an event still waiting to unfold. They cannot be computed in advance, because they have not yet happened.

And these bypassed conditions are precisely the qualification by which a person is treated as a subject who can argue back, can respond, can be understood anew. When judgment can take effect as usual while bypassing them, what is suspended is the subject's position to speak within this judgment. This, of course, we already know. What I want to raise is a further question beyond it. "Judgment" has always been taken as a single whole, its conditions and its outcome hard to pull apart. But if a "predictive system" became accurate enough, accurate enough to absorb an individual's appeals and, on that basis, actually change the outcome it gives, handing down an adjusted "perfect judgment," then has this synthetic empty judgment already come to possess the reality of "judgment"? And the sense of "being judged" that a person receives within it, what kind of synthetic artefact is that?

One line of research argues that subjects determined by an algorithm should regain channels to contest, to respond, and to demand explanations, and that once these channels are designed into the system, the subject's position to respond can be restored (Yurrita et al., 2025).[^5] But when a system becomes accurate enough to absorb these contestations and to adjust its own outcomes accordingly, I think the situation only grows worse. The more a system can respond to appeals, the more thoroughly it hollows out: each "perfect" adjustment produces a new judgment that has bypassed the constitutive conditions, and so produces more and more of an undefinable, incomplete "experience of being judged."
